inline.s: (Gui) Second, clarifying the extinction of offenses and the gaining of merit.
[“‘Because in this present life people slight and despise him, his offenses from former lives are thereby extinguished, and he shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.’”]

This section precisely clarifies that the sutra’s power is inconceivable. As for the two lines, “Because in this present life people slight and despise him, his offenses from former lives are thereby extinguished,” people of old explained them as meaning that heavy karma is turned so that it is lightly borne (see Guifeng’s Collected Essentials and Changshui’s Record of Definitive Settlement). This explanation should not be taken in a narrow sense. If taken narrowly, it clashes with the Buddha’s intent in many ways. How does it clash with what the Buddha said? Consider the preceding section: immediately after “is slighted and despised by others,” it continues, “this person’s offenses from former lives should fall into the evil paths.” This precisely shows that his being slighted and despised is brought about by former karma, and is itself the first sign of his deserving to fall into the evil paths. That no other dharma is employed to turn him about and make him so is abundantly clear. The word “extinguished” here must not be misunderstood as the two karmas of good and evil canceling each other out. The sutras constantly teach the principle that cause and effect are one and the same: “as the cause, so the fruit.” It is also said: “Though a hundred thousand kalpas pass, the karma one has made does not perish.” This suffices to show that the two karmas of good and evil each remain, and cannot cancel each other. Even in this sutra: it was said above that one who can believe it has already planted good roots at immeasurable millions of Buddhas. If they could cancel one another, his former offenses would long ago have been canceled. How could he still, in this life, deserve to fall into the evil paths? Reading the text before and after together, it is plainly easy to see that each has its own cause and effect, that each remains, and that they cannot cancel one another. But the phrase “turned so that it is lightly borne” implies cancellation. Hence I say it clashes in many ways.

This being so, what is to be done? There is only one way: to strive with all one’s might to extinguish the evil seeds. What is meant by canceling out? Take an account book: by setting the two figures of receipts and payments against each other until they cancel, one reckons only the remaining balance. Good and evil causes and effects cannot cancel out in this way; one can only reckon whatever good or evil remains, and speak of retribution accordingly. Why? In an account book, though there may be all kinds of monies, there is a universally fixed standard by which things of different kinds can be converted to one, and so they can be canceled. But the karma of good and evil differs utterly in weight and in great and small. Since there is no standard by which to measure and convert them, how can they be canceled? Hence though a hundred thousand kalpas pass, that karma does not perish.

What is meant by extinguished? Suppose a field has seeds sown long ago, rice and weeds together. Now one only cultivates the rice seeds and brings them to grain. When the weed seeds sprout, one pulls them out root and all — this is what is meant by extinguished. So too with people. In the field of the eighth consciousness, seeds both good and evil have existed since beginningless time. One need only permeate the good seeds and bring them to a good fruit; then the evil seeds have no way to arise. Even if evil seeds from former lives have already begun to develop, one need only, during the time when the evil fruit has not yet ripened, advance with courage and vigor so that the good fruit ripens first; then the evil fruit cannot suddenly come to be. If one goes on for a long time increasing good roots, then with branches and leaves spreading thick, the evil fruit long lacks any opportunity to ripen, and will rot away and be no more. This is said with reference to worldly good deeds and to the incomplete teachings of supramundane dharmas. But if one follows the most supreme, complete teaching, cultivating the supreme cause and achieving the supreme fruit, then all the evil seeds of former lives, roots and leaves together, along with their fruits that are about to ripen or have not yet ripened, can be cut off and uprooted. How much more than merely having the good fruit ripen first, so that the evil fruit cannot come to be!

The “extinguished” spoken of here is precisely this meaning. The three lines of the sutra text join in one breath and are unfolded one from another. “Extinguishing offenses” and “shall attain” cannot be taken as two separate matters. The verb “is” in “is thereby” is read in its ordinary sense. “Are thereby extinguished” takes its sense from this very extinction; the sutra’s meaning is presumably that the offenses this person committed in former lives, which deserve falling into the evil paths, though he has not yet fallen, are already on the verge of ripening their fruit. Hence there is already the first sign of being slighted and despised by others. Were he not to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, he would certainly fall. How perilous, how near to ruin! Fortunately this person has deep prajñā seeds from former lives, and can rely on this sutra, cultivate the supreme cause, separate from marks, see the nature, and leap straight in at one bound. Therefore his supreme fruit too will ripen. So one who should by rights have fallen, merely because in this present life he is slighted and despised by others, has his former offenses extinguished on the spot. For he rightly recollects true suchness, is qualified to attain unsurpassed bodhi, and clearly sees that the nature of offenses is fundamentally empty. Thus it can be seen that the line “shall attain” in the sutra is precisely what explains why the offenses are extinguished. One should know that without extinguishing offenses one certainly cannot realize the fruit. Yet the sutra says “shall attain,” not “has now attained.” Saying “shall attain” shows that his cause holds the definite possibility of realizing unsurpassed bodhi; hence even very heavy offenses, already showing the first sign of deserving a fall, can be extinguished on the spot. The “shall” of “shall attain” means “in the future,” and also “certainly shall.” Though not yet attained now, in the future he shall certainly attain it — a word of decision. “Should fall” likewise means “shall certainly fall in the future.” But because this is the supreme, ultimate fruit, there is no waiting for it to ripen first; with only the prospect of a certain ripening, the evil fruit is uprooted entirely. For what he cultivates is the work of no mark of self, no mark of dharma, and no mark of non-dharma. Since the mind that creates is empty, the karma created perishes of itself. As it is said: “Offenses arise from the mind; with the mind one repents them. When the mind is empty, offenses too are gone.” This is precisely where the sutra’s power is most fully revealed. Because people fail to grasp where the sutra’s purport lies, they mistakenly think that offenses are extinguished because of being slighted by others, and so arises the misreading that heavy karma is turned so as to be lightly borne.

In short, the two lines — “Because in this present life (read with stress) people slight and despise him, his offenses from former lives are (read with stress) thereby (read with stress) extinguished” — make clear that in later lives he will certainly not fall. The word “because” in them is precisely what awakens one to this meaning. How could it be misread as saying that if he were not slighted and despised by others, his offenses would not be extinguished! The preceding section’s statement that he is slighted and despised by others shows that fixed karma cannot be escaped. Its statements of “offenses” and “should fall” show the two obstructions of karma and retribution. And since karma and retribution come from delusion, speaking of karma and retribution includes the obstruction of delusion within it. What this section states is the removal of the three obstructions. For one who receives and upholds this sutra can contemplate the principle of the three emptinesses, and has the possibility of attaining the ultimate fruit; that his contemplation and practice are very profound is thus evident, and the obstruction of delusion can be dissolved thereby. When the root is withered the branches and leaves wilt; hence even fixed karma that cannot be escaped, which already shows the first sign of deserving a fall, has its karmic force extinguished on the spot. When the obstruction of karma is dissolved, the obstruction of retribution is dissolved along with it, and one who should fall does not fall. When the three obstructions are wholly removed, the three virtues are perfect and bright; hence it says “shall attain bodhi” — all of which serves to reveal that the sutra’s power is inconceivable. As for “shall attain”: how many lives may intervene is not fixed; it depends entirely on when his three virtues are cultivated to perfection, and then he attains. Yet though the time cannot be fixed, because the three obstructions can be removed, there will ultimately be a time of attainment, and he will beyond doubt attain it — this is what “shall attain” means. Since these two words were personally sanctioned by the World-Honored One, they are a prediction. As the text later says: Dīpaṃkara Buddha gave me a prediction: “In a future life you shall become a Buddha.” There he says “become a Buddha”; here it says “unsurpassed, perfectly enlightened” — different names, the same meaning. “Unsurpassed, perfectly enlightened” is spoken with respect to the fruit-dharma. “Buddha” is spoken with respect to the fruit-position. Realizing this fruit-dharma and ascending to the fruit-position is called Buddha. “Tathāgata” is spoken with respect to the fruit-virtue. Realizing this fruit-dharma so that the virtue of the nature is perfectly manifest is called Tathāgata. Thus it can be known that “Buddha” and “Tathāgata” include the meaning of unsurpassed, perfectly enlightened, and that “anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi” likewise includes the meanings of Buddha and Tathāgata. For apart from a Buddha, a Tathāgata, none can be called unsurpassed, perfectly enlightened. Hence these three names are all titles for the ultimate fruit of enlightenment. It is only that one reveals the ultimate dharma, another the ultimate position, another the ultimate virtue, and so three names are set up.

The World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma is skillful, perfect, and wondrous. Within a single phrase ten thousand things are encompassed. His words and sentences are like wind meeting water: wholly without deliberation, yet linked and mirrored one to another, forming a most intricate and most brilliant wondrous text. Take this very section: had it merely said, “One who receives, upholds, reads, and recites this sutra, and whose offenses from former lives deserve the evil paths, has them extinguished, and shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,” that would have sufficed to reveal the sutra’s power. Yet it brings in “is slighted and despised by others,” and “because in this present life people slight and despise him,” and so on. The meanings contained therein are then inexhaustible. Let me now briefly set out five of them:

(1) It makes one know that cause and effect are to be feared, and that evil karma must not be created. Happily one relies on the power of the Diamond Prajñā, and so escapes falling; yet even so it is hard to escape entirely.

(2) It makes those who have heard the foregoing teaching on reverence know that they must not cling to marks. Clinging to marks, when they meet with things contrary to their wishes, they will surely retreat in mind.
(3) It makes those who meet with adverse circumstances likewise not cling to marks, but contemplate the extinction of offenses.

(4) The former karma of all beings is without limit. It makes one know that even the heaviest former karma, whose retribution is about to ripen and which already shows its first sign, can be extinguished by the power of this sutra.

(5) It makes one know that the transformations of cause and effect are exceedingly complex, and that one should observe them to the very end. One must not look only at the present, and with shallow views fall into doubt.

In the section above on generating merit, three essentials were clearly shown to encourage learners. In this section on extinguishing offenses, three essentials are likewise hinted at, to admonish learners. The first essential: to be slighted and despised by others in this life is brought about by heavy offenses from former lives. Whoever meets with such a thing should give rise to a mind of fear, and should give rise to a mind that accepts it willingly. The second essential: one who is slighted and despised, if he receives, upholds, reads, and recites this sutra, can dissolve his former karma. He should give rise to a mind that takes refuge in the Diamond Prajñā, and should give rise to the mind of a good teacher toward those who slight and despise him. The third essential: being slighted and despised by others is the first sign of deserving to fall. All learners should give rise to a mind that diligently seeks repentance. And since it says “shall attain bodhi,” he has not yet attained it; he should give rise to a mind of courage and vigor.

The five brief points and the three essentials are all the gist of this section. The Sutra of the Names of the Buddhas says: “One who does good meets with obstacles in everything he touches; how much more in this age of chaos!” If one constantly uses this gist to rouse oneself, one will not, perhaps, be disturbed by circumstances and conditions.

A moment ago I spoke of diligently seeking repentance. One should know that receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting this sutra is precisely the wondrous gate of repentance. Why is this said? The Lotus Sutra says: “If one wishes to repent, let him sit upright and contemplate true suchness (to contemplate is to observe); heavy offenses are like frost and dew, and the sun of wisdom can dissolve them.” The essence of this sutra is true suchness. The sutra says: “When the mind of faith is pure, true suchness is brought forth.” A pure mind is freedom from marks and from thoughts. Freedom from marks and from thoughts is precisely the contemplation of true suchness. It is also precisely the supreme wondrous method for removing delusion, dissolving karma, and turning retribution. This is the gate of repentance in principle within the rites of repentance. The sutra further has one practice the mark-free giving and the six pāramitās for the benefit of beings. The Chapter on the Conduct and Vows says: “If a bodhisattva can accord with beings, he thereby accords with and makes offerings to all Buddhas; if he respects and serves beings, he thereby respects and serves the Tathāgata; if he causes beings to rejoice, he causes all Tathāgatas to rejoice.” Hence practicing the six pāramitās is the gate of repentance in practice within the rites of repentance. For when the ancients composed their rites of repentance, in addition to repentance in principle they had people make offerings and pay reverence and separately cultivate repentance in practice, precisely in order to permeate and rouse the mind that broadly practices the six pāramitās. How could it be that merely bowing a few times settles the matter? Looking at what this section says — that through receiving and upholding this sutra one’s former karma is extinguished — its being a wondrous gate of repentance is most evident. For “receiving and upholding” means advancing in both understanding and practice. Understanding is contemplation, which includes repentance in principle; practice includes repentance in practice. From this it can also be known that “receiving and upholding” is another name for contemplation and practice. To regard receiving and upholding as merely reading and reciting is a great mistake. For if that were so, when it says “receiving and upholding,” why does it also say “reading and reciting”? One should know that reading and reciting are originally meant to permeate and rouse receiving and upholding. If one merely reads and recites without receiving and upholding, one can only plant a distant cause and cannot reap great results; one can only increase merit and cannot open wisdom; one can only dissolve light karma and cannot extinguish heavy offenses — still less can one attain unsurpassed bodhi. This is how it should be understood.

In sum: that this sutra has inconceivable, immeasurable, boundless merit and virtue is only fully revealed at this section. And the reason why the merit of one whose faith is not contrary surpasses that other merit is likewise only thoroughly explained at this section. That this section is titled not “extinguishing offenses and receiving a prediction” but “extinguishing offenses and gaining merit” is precisely to point out that the merit that surpasses that other is only gained at this point.

This great section, which most fully reveals the sutra’s power, speaks a thousand words and ten thousand phrases, yet its one and only purport can be summed up and stated in a few words: if a student of Buddhism does not enter through this sutra, then even if he practices austerities for countless kalpas, he can only become a bodhisattva and cannot become a Buddha. This is precisely unfolding the purport of the concluding words of the earlier section on generating faith — that all Buddhas and the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi Dharma of all Buddhas come forth from this sutra — in order to urge all beings to generate faith. From this it can be seen that this sutra’s chapters and sentences are exceedingly well ordered, and its principles exceedingly interpenetrating. Earlier, when explaining the section on generating faith, I said: the one section on generating faith has already encompassed the whole sutra’s purport; thereafter it is merely a matter of taking the principles stated in generating faith and, layer by layer, giving them a broader unfolding and a deeper, more secret elaboration. Looking at the meaning made clear in this great section, this should be quite clear.
(Ren) Third, revealing by way of offering to Buddhas. Two parts: (Gui) First, clarifying the offering to Buddhas; second, revealing the upholding of the sutra.
(Gui) First, clarifying the offering to Buddhas.

[“Subhūti, I recall that in the past, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas before Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I met eight hundred and forty million billion nayutas of Buddhas, and honored them all with offerings and service, without passing by any in vain.”]

Asaṃkhyeya is here rendered “incalculable,” that is, “innumerable.” The word kalpa already refers to an extremely long span of time. To say “asaṃkhyeya kalpas” is to have passed through numberless extremely long spans of time. Not only so — it further says “immeasurable.” As the Avataṃsaka says: “Asaṃkhyeya times asaṃkhyeya makes one asaṃkhyeya-turn. Asaṃkhyeya-turn times asaṃkhyeya-turn makes one immeasurable.” That is, when the number of asaṃkhyeyas is accumulated to asaṃkhyeya-fold, it is called an asaṃkhyeya-turn; and when the number of these asaṃkhyeya-turns is accumulated to asaṃkhyeya-turn-fold, it first becomes “immeasurable.” Then the number “immeasurable” is used to reckon asaṃkhyeya kalpas. In brief, one may call it immeasurably numberless long kalpas — what is called “kalpas as numerous as dust-motes.” The number of kalpas passed through is like motes of dust, countless: not to be reckoned by calculation, not to be expressed by simile; only a Buddha can know it. All these kalpas were before Dīpaṃkara Buddha.

According to the common teaching of the doctrine, cultivation from the position of faith to the first abiding requires ten thousand kalpas — or, some say, three asaṃkhyeya kalpas. And from the first abiding to the Buddha-position likewise requires three asaṃkhyeya kalpas. There is yet another account: that from the position of faith to the Buddha-position is altogether three asaṃkhyeya kalpas. These accounts differ in many ways. Let me now cross-check them against the number of kalpas stated in this section. Our World-Honored One, at the end of the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa, met Dīpaṃkara Buddha, realized the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, and so passed from the seventh ground to the eighth ground, thereby entering the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa. On this basis, counting backward from the time he met Dīpaṃkara Buddha to the time of the first abiding, according to the doctrine there is only one — the first — asaṃkhyeya kalpa. Even reckoning the second asaṃkhyeya together with it (since the time of meeting Dīpaṃkara was at the end of the second asaṃkhyeya, it may be counted together), there are still only two asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Subtract these two from the immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas, and what remains is still immeasurable. Hence cultivation from the position of faith to the first abiding is immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas — how much more than three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and still more than ten thousand kalpas! If one reckons by the account that from the position of faith to the Buddha-position is altogether three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, the discrepancy with the number of kalpas stated in this sutra is even greater. One often sees people who, because of this, raise countless doubts. Hence I cannot but cite the matter and explain the reason for the difference.

One should know that the sutras contain such various differing accounts for a profound reason. What is that reason? What is called “skillful means suited to the faculties.” As the Lotus Sutra says: “My speaking of Dīpaṃkara Buddha was all by way of skillful means,” and so on. Worldly people often take the two words “skillful means” to mean “casual.” If someone’s words or conduct do not conform to fixed rules, they call it “skillful means.” This is not the meaning of skillful means spoken of in the sutras. In the sutras, whatever is unobstructed in principle, exactly fitting in practice, and by nature not to be rigidly adhered to, is expressed by the two words “skillful means.” Hence all skillful-means words and all skillful-means deeds are so by reason of suiting the faculties. That the number of kalpas is given in differing accounts is also this meaning. For the time elapsed from the position of faith through the first abiding to Buddhahood may be long or short, depending entirely on whether the person’s faculties are sharp or dull and whether his practice is diligent or slack — hence the differences. How could one be rigid about it? For this reason there are various differing accounts. If one understands this principle, then all similar statements in the sutras can be understood by it. One must not be stuck on them, and need not doubt them.

Dīpaṃkara, also named Dingguang, is a Buddha of ancient times. “Met” means “encountered.” “Nayuta” is here rendered as one hundred million. Taking one hundred million and multiplying it by eight hundred and forty million billion times is likewise an extreme statement of how many Buddhas he met: not to be reckoned by calculation, not to be expressed by simile; only a Buddha can know it. Since the kalpas were as long as that, he naturally met Buddhas as numerous as this.

“Offering” in brief means the four kinds of offering: food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine. In the broad sense it means the offering of things and the offering of Dharma as spoken of in the Avataṃsaka. (The offering of things extends the four items above more widely; the offering of Dharma means practicing according to the Dharma.) “Service” means attending upon him at his side. “All without passing by any in vain” refers precisely to this. “Without passing by any in vain” means there was not one Buddha whom he did not thus offer to and serve. All the above, in fully stating the length of time and the diligence of his offerings to Buddhas, serves as the groundwork for showing that these do not equal receiving and upholding this sutra.
(Gui) Second, revealing the upholding of the sutra.

[“If again there be a person who, in the latter age, the final era, can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit and virtue he obtains — compared with the merit and virtue of my offerings to those Buddhas — is not one hundredth part of it, not a thousandth, ten-thousandth, or hundred-millionth part, not even a part to be reckoned by calculation or expressed by simile.”]

“Latter” means the five hundred years after [the Buddha’s passing], which is precisely the Dharma-ending age. It also broadly refers to what comes after those five hundred years, down to their very end; hence “the latter age, the final era.” The word “than” in “than my” carries the sense of comparison. It says that his merit from upholding the sutra, compared with my merit from offering to Buddhas, is such that I am not fit to be compared with him. For the merit of offering to Buddhas is not one hundredth part of his single part — not a thousandth, ten-thousandth, or hundred-millionth part, not a part that calculation cannot compute or simile cannot express: none of them reaches a single part of his. That it says “one hundredth” and then proceeds through “a thousandth, ten-thousandth, hundred-millionth,” and parts to be reckoned by calculation or simile, is because the faculties of those who uphold the sutra are sharp or dull and their practice deep or shallow in many different ways; hence the degree to which they are not equal varies so greatly. This fifth comparison revealing the sutra’s power is stated after the extinction of offenses and the attainment of bodhi. Its meaning is as if to say: by receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting this sutra one gains the removal of obstructions and gains a prediction — how could that be reached by my having, before I received my prediction, passed through countless kalpas and met countless Buddhas, knowing only how to make offerings and serve them? For offering and serving are only reverence and toil; but to bear the Tathāgata’s burden is to continue and prosper the Buddha-seed. The greatness of compassion, wisdom, practice, and vow differs by a vast distance. Hence it says “not even a part to be reckoned by calculation or expressed by simile.” The comparison here cannot be put in terms of length of time or the speed of receiving a prediction. For the one who upholds the sutra has already planted good roots at immeasurable millions of Buddhas; the length of time and the number of Buddhas met are just the same. Nor can it be put vaguely in terms of hearing the Dharma. For since both met many Buddhas, served and made offerings to them, and planted good roots, how could they not have heard the Dharma? Hence the reason why offering and serving do not equal it points precisely at receiving and upholding this sutra. For the purport of the sutra is to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and to show the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. If one can truly receive and uphold it, one awakens to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. That is why countless gifts of the seven treasures, gifts of body and life, and many kalpas of offering to Buddhas cannot equal it — the reason lies here. Why? Because all Buddhas and the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi Dharma of all Buddhas come forth from this sutra. Hence the two words “offering” should also be explained as including the offering of Dharma; only so does it appear that this sutra cannot be matched by any dharma. It cannot be explained solely as the four kinds of offering. That he compares and reveals it by his own affair, and points out that this was before Dīpaṃkara Buddha, precisely shows that this sutra is the essential mind-transmitting Dharma handed down from Buddha to Buddha, and that it was obtained by his own many kalpas of diligent, bitter cultivation and realization — every phrase a word of one who has personally tasted sweet and bitter — in order to urge the multitude to believe and enter this gate, alike to receive the prediction and together realize bodhi.

The first four comparisons all say that his merit surpasses that other, revealing the superior by means of the inferior; hence they say “blessed merit” and not “merit and virtue.” For it shows that the superior one, since he possesses right prajñā wisdom, has all the blessed merit he cultivates become boundless merit and virtue, and therefore surpasses the other. This comparison says that the merit and virtue of offering to Buddhas does not equal upholding the sutra, revealing the inferior by means of the superior; hence it says “merit and virtue” and not “blessed merit.” It shows that the inferior one, lacking right prajñā wisdom, though not without merit and virtue, has it become only outflows-tainted blessed merit, and therefore does not equal it.
Though the sutra text says only “receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting,” it includes “widely explaining it for others.”

That it speaks of the latter age alone has four meanings. (1) Beings in the latter age are firm in strife; their karma is heavy and their merit light, their obstructions deep and their wisdom shallow — yet there are still those who receive, uphold, read, and recite. Hence it is clear that in times other than the latter age there must be many such people. So by speaking of one “latter age” it gathers up all other times: this is the skillfulness of its manner of speaking. (2) Because in such a time there are such people, it especially brings up the latter age to speak of it, in order to show that beings must not be slighted: this is the evenness of its gathering-in. (3) This sutra is most able to remove the obstruction of karma; hence it speaks of the latter age alone, because beings in such a time cannot but revere and uphold this sutra: this is the compassion of its rescue. (4) This sutra is bound up with the very lifeline of the Three Treasures; hence in bringing up the latter age to speak of it, it urges all beings present and to come to strive to spread it widely, so that to the end of the future it is not cut off: this is the depth and length of its charge.
(Ren) Fourth, concluding the sutra’s power. Two parts: (Gui) First, clarifying that it is hard to state in full; second, clarifying the inconceivable.
(Gui) First, clarifying that it is hard to state in full.

[“Subhūti, if a good man or good woman, in the latter age, should receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and I were to state in full the merit and virtue he obtains, some who heard it would have their minds go wild and confused, and would waver in doubt and not believe.”]

This section concluding the sutra’s power is the summary conclusion of the first half. It not only concludes the section on opening understanding; it not only concludes the first half, but also gives rise to the second half. Of its two small sections, the first, on the difficulty of stating it in full, concludes the five preceding comparisons revealing merit; the second, on the inconceivable, concludes the true purport of the first half and thereby gives rise to the second half. Both small sections contain two profound meanings: admonishing learners and revealing the sutra’s purport. Its chapters and sentences are exceedingly well ordered, its true principle exceedingly complete. Let me explain it layer by layer:

How do we know it is meant to admonish learners? Consider what was said above: that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, rare Dharma; and further, generating merit, extinguishing offenses, bearing the Tathāgata’s burden, and attaining bodhi — the merit and virtue obtained has already been fully stated. Why then does it say here that it has not been stated in full? Again, above it was said that this sutra has inconceivable merit and virtue, and that such a person’s accomplishing the bearing of the Tathāgata’s burden and attaining bodhi is itself the inconceivability of the retribution. These two kinds of inconceivability were long ago clearly stated to let the multitude know them. Why then does it say here again, “you should know”? Its meaning is evidently different from before. For these words concluding the sutra’s power are not spoken to urge faith, but carry the sense of admonition. “Mad and bewildered,” “doubting,” and “you should know” are all words admonishing learners.

What is meant by “mad and bewildered”? “Mad” means wildly presumptuous; it refers to those who recklessly talk of prajñā. Why is their talk reckless? Because they have not understood the true meaning. With the true meaning unclear, one will inevitably speak of dharmas as non-dharmas and of non-dharmas as dharmas, confounding the minds of the multitude — not only confounding one’s own mind. Hence it says “their minds go mad and bewildered.” What is meant by “doubting”? It means half-believing, half-disbelieving. This refers to those who fear to talk of prajñā; they too, through not understanding the true meaning, are terrified, doubtful, and afraid, and cannot give rise to settled faith. Hence it says “doubting and not believing.” The World-Honored One, foreseeing from afar that beings in the latter age would have these two ailments, therefore in the next section earnestly admonishes them, saying, “you should know,” and so on.
“If I were to state it in full” means that it is hard to state in full. This contains two meanings:

(1) It explains why the comparison is made in five stages and not stated in full all at once. It means: had I not gone from shallow to deep, revealing it stage by stage, but had stated the sutra’s power in full at one time, it would not only be hard to explain, but would certainly make some hearers mad and others doubtful, adding fault on top of fault. For those of sharp faculties often see things too easily; hearing the merit and virtue stated in full, they become wildly conceited — claiming realization where there is no realization, claiming attainment where there is no attainment — and confound the minds of the multitude. And those of dull faculties often cling to marks and fear difficulty: having heard that all is non-dwelling, and then hearing the merit and virtue stated in full, they dare not affirm it as right nor dare to deny it as wrong; they waver in doubt, unable to decide, and do not give rise to faith. The World-Honored One’s speaking thus is to admonish those who hear the sutra’s power revealed that they should thoroughly grasp the reason why it proceeds from shallow to deep; then they will not, muddled about true suchness, give rise to a wildly presumptuous mind, nor, failing to understand the sutra’s purport, give rise to a doubting mind.

(2) It explains why, having already explained it five times, it is no longer stated in full. It means: my extensive speaking above of the merit and virtue gained by one who receives and upholds this sutra was intended only to show and urge; hereafter I will say no more of it. I fear hearers may not understand the intent: some may cling to marks and seek, and so their minds go mad and bewildered; some, not gaining it at once, may instead waver in doubt and not believe. The World-Honored One’s speaking thus is to admonish practitioners that they should know this matter is by nature beyond what words reach, and only realization can know it. One must be wholly unattached, truly cultivate and truly practice; only after long time can one accord with it — one must not be wild. When the work is done one knows of oneself; there is no need to doubt. For this reason the second half’s comparisons revealing the sutra’s power only briefly suggest the meaning, not as emphatically as before. For the first half is precisely to cause the generation of faith and the opening of understanding: if it were not revealed with all one’s might, how could one believe? How could one understand? The second half is precisely to cause cultivation and realization in the direction of freedom from names and cutting off marks. Even bodhi-mind, bodhi-dharma, and bodhi-fruit should not be clung to — how much less merit and virtue. If it were again spoken of extensively, it would obstruct cultivation and realization. Yet it is also not absolutely unspoken of, which again shows that one should merely not cling, and that it is not annihilation. “Some” expresses the deep hope that such people will not be many.
(Gui) Second, clarifying the inconceivable.
[“Subhūti, you should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its retribution is also inconceivable.”]

The two words “you should know” are precisely words admonishing the mad and the doubtful. Why are they mad? Why do they doubt? Because they do not know that the purport of this sutra and the retribution gained by upholding and teaching it are both inconceivable. Hence the admonition “you should know.” “Retribution” covertly refers to the merit and virtue obtained. The merit and virtue obtained is nothing else than what the text above calls bearing the Tathāgata’s burden and attaining bodhi.

What is meant by “the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable”? One should know that the purport of this sutra is devoted to clarifying freedom from all marks: only by freedom from marks can one realize the nature. As it is said, “free from names and cut off from marks; only realization can know it.” Hence it says the sutra’s meaning is inconceivable. What is meant by “its retribution is also inconceivable”? One should know that receiving and upholding this sutra is originally for the sake of realizing the nature. To realize the nature that is neither with marks nor without marks, and in which marks and no-marks are both absent, one must be free from all marks. With each degree of freedom, there is each degree of realization. The retribution is nothing else than this: personally realizing the ultimate, with the virtue of the nature perfectly manifest. Hence it says the retribution too is inconceivable. In sum, it shows that the sutra’s meaning and its retribution can neither be thought nor discussed; in every case one should be free from the marks of names, of words, and of mental activity, and enter subtly and secretly. If one can know this, then while false clinging is not yet dispelled, how could one be arrogant? The mad and bewildered mind can be put to rest. When empty marks are wholly dispelled, the pure virtue shows itself of itself; the doubting mind can be released.

Earlier, in the section on extinguishing offenses, I said: the full revelation of the sutra’s power is precisely an unfolding of the purport stated in the earlier section on generating faith — that all Buddhas and the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi Dharma of all Buddhas come forth from this sutra — in order to urge faith. This concluding section, being the summary conclusion of that full revelation, is precisely an unfolding of the words that follow “come forth from this sutra,” namely the purport that what are called Buddha and Dharma are not Buddha and Dharma, in order to open understanding. The World-Honored One’s meaning is as if to say: why was it said above that Dharma is not Dharma? One should know it is because the sutra’s meaning is inconceivable. Why was it said above that Buddha is not Buddha? One should know it is because the retribution too is inconceivable. For “is not,” in brief, means “freedom from marks.”

In fullest terms: the essence of the nature is empty and still, and not the least mote of a mark can be clung to. Cling, and it is no longer the empty, still essence of the nature. Hence it says “is not.” The reason I made the five stages of revealing the sutra’s power and did not wish to state it in full was to enable hearers to grasp it deeply in mind: merit and virtue differ according to how shallow or deep one’s freedom from marks is. So they will not talk of emptiness with the mouth while clinging to marks in the mind, and so become wildly presumptuous and confuse themselves; nor, on hearing of freedom from marks, fear one-sided emptiness and waver in doubt and disbelief. In sum, the purport of this sutra is devoted to dispelling emotional clinging in order to realize the empty, still nature. What is called retribution is precisely the realization of the nature that cannot be thought of or referred to. Only when the way of words is cut off and the activity of the mind is extinguished can one be said to accord with it in some small measure. The activity of the mind extinguished — that is the inconceivable. The way of words cut off — that is the inexpressible. This is what is meant by “the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its retribution is also inconceivable.” This is what is meant by “Buddha and Dharma are not Buddha and Dharma.” If one does not know to contemplate and enter within this cutting off of the way of words, this extinction of the activity of the mind, this inconceivability, then one turns away from the sutra’s meaning, and how could any retribution be realized? There would be only madness and doubt. Those who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra should know it thus.

“Knowing” is “understanding.” These words serve as the general conclusion of the whole great section on opening understanding. They precisely show that what is called opening understanding means understanding deeply in this way. They also precisely show that the purport of this whole great section on opening understanding is to guide learners step by step and bring them to such deep understanding. Truly these are the words that dot the eye of the painted dragon. In sum, they show that cultivation takes the opening of understanding as its root. Arising practice in accord with understanding, one can then achieve the supreme fruit. Otherwise, one is either mad or doubtful. Its instruction is earnest, its admonition profound. Yet among the beings of the last age who read and recite this sutra, those who fall into these two ailments are by no means few. Because they mostly overlook the reason for the five comparisons revealing the sutra’s power, they cannot deeply and clearly understand even the principle set forth in this concluding section. Muddled and vague — do they not deeply betray the Buddha’s kindness?

Since the section that most fully reveals the sutra’s power unfolds the purport of “all Buddhas” down to “are not Buddha and Dharma,” this concluding section here not only fully concludes the purport of the section on opening understanding, but fully concludes the purport of the section on generating faith as well. For without thus using a later meaning to reveal an earlier meaning, the purport of the first half could not be unfolded thoroughly. (“All Buddhas” and the rest is the summary conclusion of the whole great section on generating faith; the section most fully revealing the sutra’s power is the summary conclusion of the whole great section on opening understanding. Now by using the later summary to reveal the earlier summary, the purport of the first half is doubly manifested, and the guiding threads are in hand.) Nor could it give rise to the second half. For the text of the second half is precisely devoted to clarifying the cultivation and realization that consists in the cutting off of the way of words, the extinction of the activity of the mind, and the inconceivable. Hence the sutra text before and after is linked and locked by these two words, “you should know”; chapter arrangement and principle are joined into one continuous whole. How could one narrowly say the first half is shallow and the second deep? These two lines refer to the whole sutra together, and closely join on to the second half. How could one narrowly judge the first and second halves as two separate rounds of teaching, as though each had nothing to do with the other? As for regarding what the second half says as largely repetitive — that shows far too little grasp of the sutra’s purport, and is not worth discussing!
The one phrase “inconceivable” has three meanings:

(1) It is exactly what was said above: the way of words cut off, the activity of the mind extinguished. What the sutra’s meaning clarifies is this; what the retribution obtains is this. This is the primary meaning.

(2) It echoes back to the line that this sutra has inconceivable merit and virtue and the like, and adds an explanation, thereby gathering up the section that most fully reveals the sutra’s power. Above it merely said the sutra has such merit and virtue. Now it explains: saying the sutra has it is because its teaching is thus. (The earlier judgment that the teaching is superior is grounded in these words here.) How does one know the teaching has such merit and virtue? Because those who practice in accord with the teaching can obtain such a retribution. “Inconceivable” is the dharmakāya, is the essence. (See the earlier explanation.) Only having the essence can one give rise to function. Having realized the dharmakāya, the reward and transformation bodies show themselves of themselves. Hence merely saying “inconceivable” suffices; there is no need to say “immeasurable” and the like. Moreover, since it also clarifies the primary meaning of the cutting off of the way of words and the extinction of the activity of the mind, no other words could be mixed in.

(3) It reveals that the merit and virtue of this sutra and the merit and virtue of those who uphold it are supreme, without equal, not to be peered at by ordinary feelings, not to be spoken by words. Hence though it says only “inconceivable,” it covertly includes within it the meanings “immeasurable” and “boundless” — supremely skillful.

To discuss this division in detail: it has two general sections. The first clarifies non-dwelling with respect to objects, in order to manifest right prajñā wisdom — this is the first half of the sutra already explained above. The second clarifies non-dwelling with respect to the mind, in order to reveal the essence of prajñā principle — this is the second half of the sutra to be explained below. As for how the second half differs from the first, I should first explain the reason for it before explaining the sutra text, so that on entering the text it will be easier to grasp. And I will explain it from many sides, in hopes of making it thoroughly clear.

(1) The first half is spoken for those about to bring forth the great mind and cultivate. It teaches them how to bring forth the mind, how to deliver beings, how to subdue delusion, how to cut off delusion. The second half is spoken for those who have already brought forth the great mind and cultivate. For when one brings forth the mind and says, “I can bring it forth, I can deliver, I can subdue and cut off delusion,” this itself is still discrimination, still clinging to self, and must still be dispelled. The second half is devoted to clarifying this meaning. One should know that wherever there is grasping, one is bound and fettered by it and cannot be liberated. Ordinary people, through the clinging to a person-self (that is, grasping the physical body as self), are bound by birth and death and cannot escape the round of rebirth. The Two Vehicles, through the clinging to a dharma-self (though they do not grasp the physical body, they grasp the dharmas of the five aggregates, and their view of self is not yet forgotten; hence it is called a dharma-self), are confined by nirvāṇa, so that they sink into emptiness and stagnate in stillness. A bodhisattva, with great compassion and great wisdom, is fettered by nothing; hence without hindrance or obstruction, and at ease. This is what is called the way of non-dwelling. Therefore even a little clinging feeling should be washed utterly clean, and one should dwell in nothing at all.

(2) The clinging to a person-self and the clinging to a dharma-self, in brief, are called the clinging to self and the clinging to dharmas. It is commonly said that this sutra breaks the clinging to self in its first part and the clinging to dharmas in its latter part. This is rather loose. The first half says at the very outset: a bodhisattva should dwell in nothing with respect to dharmas; as well as no mark of self, no mark of dharma, and no mark of non-dharma; one should not grasp dharmas, one should not grasp non-dharmas; even dharmas should be relinquished, how much more non-dharmas — and so on, said again and again. How can one say it breaks only the clinging to a person-self? One should know that both the clinging to self and the clinging to dharmas are coarse and fine. The coarse is called the discriminated clinging to self and dharmas, for it arises from discrimination when facing objects and meeting conditions. The fine is called the innate clinging to self and dharmas; this does not wait upon discrimination — as soon as a thought arises it is there, born together with the thought. The first half of this sutra dispels the coarse clinging. For example: one should not dwell in the six dusts when giving; one should not bring forth a mind dwelling in the six dusts; one should have a mind of non-dwelling; one should bring forth a mind of non-dwelling; one should be free from all marks — and so on. All of these dispel the ailment of dwelling and clinging that arises from producing a discriminating mind upon objects and conditions. This is what is called the clinging to self and dharmas arising from discrimination; hence it is coarse. How is it dispelled? By freedom from marks. The second half dispels the fine clinging, that is, one should not dwell or cling even as thoughts arise and move. If a thought is retained, then the emotional thinking of the clinging to self and dharmas is not transformed, and this becomes the root of the ailment of grasping marks and clinging to objects. This is to dispel the clinging to self and dharmas that is born together with mental thoughts; hence it is fine. How is it dispelled? By freedom from thoughts.

(3) The first half’s enjoining freedom from marks is to dispel what is clung to; the second half’s enjoining freedom from thoughts is to dispel the clinging itself. Did it not say above? The illusory marks that are clung to arise from the false views that cling. Hence at first glance the purport of this sutra is shallow in front and deep behind. Yet one cannot view it so narrowly, because in dispelling what is clung to, it has already covertly dispelled the clinging as well. Why? Because without freedom from thoughts there is no way to be free from marks. Hence though the first half does not explicitly speak of freedom from thoughts, it has in fact awakened one to it in no small measure. For example: “Can one form such a thought?”, “I do not form this thought,” “one should bring forth a pure mind,” “one should bring forth a mind of non-dwelling,” “if the mind dwells, then it is not dwelling” — all of these enjoin freedom from thoughts. Even the words “one should bring forth the bodhi-mind free from all marks” — a person of sharp faculties can grasp that the mind thus brought forth should also not dwell. Why? Because it clearly says that if there is dwelling, it is not. It was said above that one whose faith is not contrary bears the Tathāgata’s burden and shall attain bodhi; such a person must already have grasped freedom from thoughts. Otherwise he could not be said to bear the burden and to attain. Hence the ancients judged that the second half was spoken for those of dull faculties — this was their meaning. They meant that those of sharp faculties have no need of its being said again. Because those of sharp faculties are few in the world, the second half had to be spoken, so that those of dull faculties might enter deeply. This was the ancients’ meaning. But because of these words one must not misunderstand and take the second half to be shallower than the first. Nevertheless, the work of freedom from thoughts is very deep and very fine. If one does not cut into it layer by layer, not only will ordinary people find it hard to advance; even those of sharp faculties who already know freedom from thoughts, if they do not polish it finely, how can their practice be thorough? It is like peeling a banana tree: without peeling and peeling again, how can one penetrate to its fundamental emptiness and return to nothing attained? One should know that in the second half, from the clarification of the five eyes onward, the more it speaks the finer it becomes. As for the section on realization, it is precisely the most direct and immediate work for entering at the tip of a single hair — what is called pointing directly upward. Without understanding this, one may be round and complete, but one is not yet sudden. To narrowly say that the second half was spoken solely for those of dull faculties does not fully accord with the sutra’s purport either. This principle must not go unknown.

(4) The first half says that only by being free from all marks does one bring forth the bodhi-mind, and only so is one a bodhisattva who benefits all beings. This empties the ailment of dwelling and clinging to self and dharmas. The second half then says: there is no dharma that brings forth bodhi, no dharma called a bodhisattva, and all dharmas are Buddha-Dharma, and so on. This empties the ailment of dwelling and clinging to the twofold emptiness of self and dharmas. Hence the first half is non-dwelling in the two extremes; the second half is non-dwelling in the two extremes and non-dwelling in that too. The first is that the mind brought forth should be free from marks; the second is that even the mark of bringing forth the mind is also relinquished. One should know that so long as the thought of being able to be free remains, self and dharmas are still plainly there, and one has already discriminated and grasped marks. Hence it also says that it is not that one does not attain bodhi by the perfection of marks; that the view of self is then no view of self; that the mark of dharma is then no mark of dharma. All of this is to sweep away subtle clinging feelings — dispelling and dispelling again, until both the clinging and that which clings are free, and even the freedom is free. Only then does one realize the original. What is called realization is nothing else: simply exhaust ordinary feelings, and the original essence shows itself — there is no separate realizing and realized. Not only must ordinary feelings not be present; even noble understanding should be absent. To retain a cultivating and cultivated, a realizing and realized, is noble understanding, which is the obstruction of the known, precisely obstructing the essence of enlightenment. Hence Maitreya Bodhisattva’s verses on the Diamond Sutra say: “Cultivating within the mind, retaining ‘I am a bodhisattva’ — this obstructs the mind and goes against the way of non-dwelling.” The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All bodhisattvas and beings of the last age should keep far from all illusory, phantom, false, and vain realms.” The first half of this sutra is nothing beyond this meaning. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment also says: “Because one firmly holds to the mind of keeping far away, the mind that is like an illusion is also kept far from; the keeping far away, being illusory, is also kept far from; the illusion of keeping far from the keeping far away is also kept far from; when one reaches having nothing to keep far from, all illusions are removed.” The second half of this sutra is nothing beyond this meaning.

(5) The first half clarifies that all is “not” (as when it says, “non-dharmas and not non-dharmas,” “if there is dwelling, then it is non-dwelling”), in order to reveal the singular truth of right prajñā wisdom. For this wisdom is by nature unstained by a single dust, whereas all marks are nothing but illusory. Hence one should not dwell in anything, and only then does right wisdom shine forth perfectly. The second half clarifies that all is “is” (as when it says, “all dharmas are the meaning of suchness,” “all dharmas are Buddha-Dharma,” “this dharma is equal, without high or low”), in order to clarify the one suchness of the essence of prajñā principle. For this essence is the source of all dharmas, and hence all dharmas are nothing but true suchness; therefore even bodhi should not be dwelt in, and only then is the essence of principle perfectly fused.

From this it is seen that the whole Diamond Sutra expounds nothing but the two words “true suchness.” It concludes at the end: “Do not grasp at marks; be unmoved in suchness.” The whole sutra’s purport is entirely contained therein. Further, the first half clarifies that all is “not,” causing one to contemplate the unchanging essence; what is called right wisdom is the wisdom of suchness, the wisdom that is the essence. The second half clarifies that all is “is,” causing one to contemplate the functioning that follows conditions; what is called the essence of principle — “principle” meaning pattern and order, spoken with respect to the functioning of the nature, and functioning is not apart from essence, hence “essence of principle.” This is utterly different from the Song Confucians’ talk of principle and vital force. They took the undifferentiated single source as principle and the flowing into ten thousand differences as vital force. Later Confucians who refuted the errors of their talk of principle did so in detail. Further: since the first half has all as “not,” although “is not” and “is named” are spoken of together, the meaning inclines to “is not” — this is what is meant by “though following conditions, unchanging.” Since the second half has all as “is,” although it finely dispels the clinging to dharmas, it says “with respect to dharmas, do not speak of the mark of annihilation” — this is what is meant by “though unchanging, following conditions.” Summing up these five explanations and viewing the whole sutra thereby, the whole sutra’s purport will be clear in mind and eye, and not merely easier to grasp on entering the text.

(Ji) Second, clarifying non-dwelling with respect to the mind in order to reveal the essence of prajñā principle. Two parts: (Geng) First, deeply contemplating non-dwelling in order to advance in practice; second, exhausting non-dwelling in order to accomplish realization. (Geng) First, again three: (Xin) First, no dharma in bringing forth the mind; second, citing the fruit to clarify the cause; third, revealing the supreme and concluding with exhortation. (Xin) First, again four: (Ren) First, asking again; second, showing the teaching; third, questioning and explaining; fourth, concluding.
(Ren) First, asking again.
[Then Subhūti said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, when a good man or good woman brings forth the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, how should he dwell? How should he subdue his mind?”]

This section looks like a fresh start, but in fact it follows closely on the preceding text. “Then” refers precisely to the moment when the Buddha had just finished saying that the sutra’s meaning and its retribution are both inconceivable. The Elder’s thought was: since one should be free from names and cut off from marks, yet good men and good women plainly each have the mark of bringing forth the mind, and there plainly is the name “anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.” For each knows for himself that he should bring forth the mind, and each knows for himself that anuttara-bodhi is the supreme dharma. Are not the names and marks of self and dharmas plainly there? It was said above that one should bring forth the bodhi-mind free from all marks; now, when one thinks of bringing forth the mind, one is at once dwelling in marks. How is it that this mind alone should dwell? If it should not dwell but should be subdued, does that not mean not bringing forth the mind? Then how should one subdue his mind? The meaning is that the two clingings to self and dharmas are already born together with the very moment of bringing forth the bodhi-mind. To subdue is not to bring forth the mind; to dwell is to cling to self and dharmas. This is precisely boring in at the tip of a single hair, instructing practitioners to apply effort at the very moment thoughts arise and move. The Elder, in great compassion, therefore asks again on behalf of all beings for the instruction of the fundamental skillful means.

Formerly it asked, “How should one abide?” — asking how the bodhi-mind should be settled, so that it does not scatter. Now it asks, “In what should one abide?” — asking how the bodhi-mind alone should dwell and cling. For if one does not dwell in this dharma, what is meant by bringing forth this mind? Dwelling is not permissible, subduing is not attainable — what then is one to do? This is because, having heard it said that one should dwell in nothing with respect to dharmas, and even that if there is dwelling it is not, one thinks that bodhi too is a dharma, and in what then should one abide? Moreover it was said above that one should bring forth the bodhi-mind free from all marks; “all marks” is very broad in scope, and the mark of bringing forth the bodhi-mind should be included in it. Why, then, having said one should be free from all marks, does it also say “bring forth the bodhi-mind”? If that too should be relinquished, why is it called bringing forth the bodhi-mind? People of dull faculties, hearing the Dharma, often cling to names and words and are stuck fast without transformation. The Elder’s question here is again asked in accommodation of all those present and to come who are stuck fast and untransformed, requesting instruction.
(Ren) Second, showing the teaching.

[The Buddha told Subhūti, “A good man or good woman who brings forth anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should thus bring forth this mind: ‘I should deliver all beings into nirvāṇa; and when all beings have been delivered into nirvāṇa, not one being has in truth been delivered into nirvāṇa.’”]

This precisely shows and teaches the skillful means of being free from marks at the moment thoughts arise and move. Look at the wording of the question in the section above: it seems there is no way out; look at the answer in this section: it is exceedingly relaxed and perfectly wondrous. After “bodhi,” the Tang-dynasty manuscript of the sutra has no word “mind,” and one should follow it. Consider: to open with the words “one who brings forth anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi” and immediately continue, “should thus bring forth this mind,” is precisely to sweep away the mark that this is bringing forth the bodhi-mind. Hence the original text does not use the word “mind,” to show the intent of effacing marks. Even in terms of the wording, it reads well without “mind.” For to bring forth anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is to bring forth unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; what objection is there to doing without the word “mind”?

The two words “thus” refer to the three sentences that follow. The word “should” in “I should” precisely echoes the word “bring forth.” For manifesting what is originally possessed is called “coming forth”; revealing what is originally absent is called “arousing.” All beings are originally of one substance; to deliver all beings into nirvāṇa is merely to complete what is inherent in one’s own share of the nature — a bounden duty — what is so extraordinary about it? If one thinks, “I ought to arouse this mind,” then there is a sense of self-display, and one clings to marks. Hence it does not say “should arouse” but “should bring forth” — for this reason. For to speak the word “should” is to dispel clinging to bodhi, breaking the clinging to dharmas; to speak “should bring forth” is to dispel clinging to the arousing of the mind, breaking the clinging to self.

The word “should” runs through the three sentences that follow. Their meaning advances in stages, each deeper than the last. The first sentence says that delivering beings is a duty one ought to fulfill; beneath the words lies the sense: how could one be self-satisfied that this is bodhi? The second says one should deliver beings to the very last; “last” means “exhausted.” Beneath the words lies the sense: beings are endless, so how could this duty ever be exhausted? How then could one claim, “I can deliver”? The third advances a step further. It says one should know that though they are delivered to the very last, there is not — (a slight pause at “not”) — in truth one single being delivered into nirvāṇa. Why? Because the nature of beings is itself nirvāṇa; and moreover, though it is nirvāṇa, it too does not dwell. For if it dwelt, it would not be deliverance into nirvāṇa. How then could there be one being in truth delivered into nirvāṇa? How then could one claim to have delivered anything?

One who brings forth unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment must first awaken to the fact that delivering beings is a duty to be fulfilled, and that this duty can never in the end be exhausted; even if exhausted, it is the same as not exhausted. One should bring forth such a mind: no deliverer, nothing delivered, no discrimination, no such thing as bodhi, no such thing as deliverance, and no such thing as bringing forth the mind. Only thus can one accord with the pure mind of enlightenment.

The earlier answer said, “in truth there are no beings who attain deliverance into nirvāṇa,” laying stress on the word “attain”: though they attain deliverance into nirvāṇa, in truth nothing is attained. Here the stress is on the words “deliverance into nirvāṇa”: there is not even anything called deliverance into nirvāṇa, so how could there be any question of attaining or not attaining? Its meaning is evidently deeper than before. Again, the earlier answer also dispelled both the deliverer and the delivered; and although that dispelling of deliverer and delivered was also a dispelling of clinging to the bodhi-mind, its tone was veiled and inclusive. Now it says deeply, clearly, and explicitly: one should bring forth just such and such a mind — so that even the shadow of “this is bodhi,” “this is bringing forth the bodhi-mind,” “this is the deliverance of beings” is not permitted to exist in the least. Hence though the words resemble the earlier answer, the meaning is like a ten-thousand-fathom pool, clear to the very bottom.

There is something further one should know. Having heard what is said here, one should begin cultivation accordingly. It was said above: the one section on generating faith has already gathered up the whole sutra’s purport; thereafter comes a broader clarification and a deeper, more secret unfolding. We learners should take up the deep and secret, and only so can we reach the ultimate. Hence those who have heard the first half of the sutra must not fail to hear the second half as well. That this sutra is naturally divided into the four parts of faith, understanding, practice, and realization does not mean that faith and understanding contain no work of practice; it indicates that all the practice-work that has come before should be cultivated in accord with what is said here. This is why, earlier, when explaining “the mind of faith is pure,” I strove to bring out that though faith, understanding, practice, and realization have an order, one must not be confined to that order; though divided into four items, one must not be confined to four. All good teachers should take this meaning to heart.
(Ren) Third, questioning and explaining.
[“Why? If a bodhisattva has the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of a being, or the mark of a life, then he is not a bodhisattva.”]

After “Why?” the circulating editions have the three words “Subhūti”; the ancient text does not, and it may be omitted. “Why?” is his own inquiry as to why one should bring forth such a mind. What follows is spoken in reverse to explain the meaning. It means: if one does not bring forth such a mind, then there is dualistic discrimination. Since one has not escaped the marks of discriminating clinging to self and others, one is still an ordinary person — how could one be a bodhisattva? The “why is this?” below further explains the reason why he is then not a bodhisattva. It was said above that if one grasps the mark of dharma, one clings to self, person, being, and life. If one thinks oneself to be bringing forth the bodhi-mind, one grasps and clings to the bodhi-dharma, and the four marks are plainly there. Hence it says, “then he is not a bodhisattva.” Therefore one should bring forth such a mind.

The four marks of self, person, being, and life, though the same as before, have a very fine meaning here. For one has already become unattached to everything, and clings only to the exceedingly subtle discrimination of seeking above and transforming below. They must not be lumped together with the ordinary four marks. The World-Honored One says this to instruct practitioners that if subtle discrimination is not purified, the root of the ailment of self-mark is still there. Though called a bodhisattva, the name does not match the reality. How profound is the intent to warn and spur on!
(Ren) Fourth, concluding.
[“Why is this? Subhūti, there is in truth no dharma that brings forth anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”]

The ancient text likewise has no word “mind” after “bodhi.” This sentence precisely introduces what follows — that there is no dharma by which one attains bodhi — and the word “mind” especially should not be there. “Why is this?” links what precedes and gives rise to what follows, concluding the meaning of the two sections above. “There is in truth no dharma that brings forth anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi” has two meanings and may be read in two ways:

(1) Pause after the word “dharma.” It means: for one who brings forth right enlightenment, there is in truth no dharma. For unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is precisely the meaning of ultimate purity. In the pure enlightenment not a single dust is stained. If the least bit remains — “this is bodhi” — then it is a dust of dharma, and not pure enlightenment. What is then brought forth is called bodhi but is in fact a discriminating mind. Hence only when there is in truth no dharma is one called one who brings forth unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

(2) Pause after the word “no.” It means: that there should be a dharma that brings forth unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment — in truth there is no such fact or principle. For beings, through unenlightenment since beginningless time, give rise to grasping out of craving, and so come to wander in birth and death. Hence no dharma whatsoever should be grasped; to grasp is to be unenlightened. How could that be called bringing forth enlightenment? Hence there is in truth no such thing as taking a dharma to be the bringing forth of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Once these two meanings are clear, the reason why the text above says “should thus bring forth this mind” and “if there are the four marks, then he is not a bodhisattva” becomes clear.

What has been clarified above is nothing other than this: one who brings forth bodhi should bring it forth without thinking himself to be bringing it forth. Such bringing forth without bringing forth is true bringing forth. And dwelling and subduing are contained therein. For how one should dwell and subdue depends entirely on how the mind is brought forth; there is no need to seek elsewhere, and hence no separate answer is given. One should know that “should thus bring forth this mind” is the meaning of dwelling without dwelling. “I should deliver all beings into nirvāṇa” and the two sentences following are the meaning of subduing the mind.

The first question was answered only with subduing and dwelling; the repeated question is answered only with bringing forth the mind — this is indeed to show the order of shallow and deep. (If one does not bring forth the mind, why ask about subduing and dwelling? Hence bringing forth the mind is the root, subduing and dwelling the branch. Hence the order of shallow and deep.) Yet the earlier answer on subduing and dwelling includes bringing forth the mind within it; and the present answer on bringing forth the mind includes subduing and dwelling within it. Moreover, if one knows how to subdue, one knows how to dwell. This again shows that the three matters are but one matter: the earlier one, spoken from the side of subduing, is originally a subduing that does not subdue; the present one, spoken from the side of bringing forth the mind, is again a bringing forth that does not bring forth. These are all subtle methods for breaking the self and dispelling clinging; one should wholeheartedly grasp them at just such points to be a good practitioner.

(Xin) Second, citing the fruit to clarify the cause. Two parts: (Ren) First, detailed clarification; second, concluding revelation. (Ren) First, again two: (Gui) First, clarifying the fruit; second, clarifying the cause. (Gui) First, again two: (Zi) First, clarifying attainment without attainment; second, clarifying that every dharma is suchness. (Zi) First, again three: (Chou) First, raising the question; second, answering and explaining; third, confirming.
(Chou) First, raising the question.
[“Subhūti, what do you think? When the Tathāgata was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, was there any dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”]

This cites a past event as proof. At that time he realized the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas and ascended to the eighth ground. The circumstances of the event have already been explained in detail above. Looking upward to the ultimate fruit, the eighth ground is still a causal stage; looking downward to those who bring forth the mind, it is a fruition stage. This matter lies between cause and effect. The principle that cause and effect are one suchness is easy to understand, and hence it is cited as proof. The World-Honored One, to guard against those who heard the above and doubted, “If bringing forth the mind involves no dharma, how does one attain the fruit?”, cites the fruit to prove it. If one knows that attaining the fruit is attaining without attainment, then bringing forth the mind must be bringing forth without bringing forth — this is clear. The section heading “citing the fruit to clarify the cause” contains both cause and effect. For it cites the fruit-dharma of the Buddha-ground to clarify the causal mind of the eighth ground; that is, by means of the mind of one at the eighth-ground fruition, it clarifies the practice of one who is first bringing forth the beginner’s enlightenment.
This matter is cited twice, before and after, with different intents. The differences of intent are three:

(1) The earlier question asked whether he attained anything with respect to dharmas; the answer was, “with respect to dharmas he in truth attained nothing.” Its meaning stresses the word “attain,” showing that though he attained, he did not dwell in the mark of attainment. This is consistent with the meaning above that the four fruits attain the mark of non-attainment, and serves to introduce what follows — that one who brings forth the mind should bring forth a pure mind and should not dwell in the marks of form, sound, and the six dusts. Here, however, the stress is on the word “dharma,” for by “no dharma attains bodhi” it proves the meaning above that no dharma brings forth bodhi.

(2) The word “dharma” in the earlier question refers to the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas. The word “dharma” here refers to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. At that time he had just ascended to the eighth ground and had not yet attained the ultimate fruit-dharma. One should know that the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas is called a limb of bodhi; it is a partial realization of bodhi, not the ultimate realization of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Hence the intent of the question here actually inclines toward the reverse and direct explanations that follow. The meaning is that because at that time, through realizing the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, not one dharma arose, he received the prediction; hence it may be known that at that time his mind did not dwell in dharmas. Because at that time his mind did not dwell in dharmas, today he has perfectly realized the ultimate fruit-dharma and become the Tathāgata. This makes one clearly understand that as the cause, so the fruit, without the slightest deviation. Then that one who brings forth the mind should not dwell in the bodhi-dharma is utterly beyond doubt.

If one misunderstands this sentence to mean that at that time he had already attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment but did not dwell in the mark of dharma, then one is far off. Consider what follows — “if there were a dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi” — which suffices to prove that the word “attain” in this sentence does not refer to that time; for at that time he had not yet become the Tathāgata. In sum: “attain” means “shall attain,” not “has already attained.”

(3) The earlier question, whether he attained anything with respect to dharmas, was likewise citing the fruit to clarify the cause. But since the word “dharma” there refers to the non-arising of dharmas, it contains only the one meaning of citing the eighth-ground fruit to clarify the causal bringing forth of the mind. The “dharma” here refers to unsurpassed bodhi, and hence it should be explained with a twofold cause and effect, and only then is the meaning complete.

“Was there any dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?” is to be read as one sentence. “There is a dharma” means the mind has that dharma, that is, the sense of dwelling in a dharma. The intent of the question is as if to say: in the past, when the Tathāgata was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, did his mind retain the fruit-dharma of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, seeking to realize it? It is like asking whether his mind retained the thought that he should attain unsurpassed bodhi. The sutra does not put it that way, but says “there is a dharma by which he attained” and so on, in order to match the earlier phrase “there is a dharma that brings forth,” so that the intent of dispelling subtle clinging to dharmas may be clear at a glance.

To speak of “a Tathāgata” already contains the sense that one should not dwell in dharmas. Tathāgata is a title of the virtue of the nature. When the enlightened nature is perfect and bright, how could there be a dust of dharma? It is so when one becomes a Buddha; then when formerly on the eighth ground, since he had received the prediction of becoming a Buddha, it may be known that his mind had no dust of dharma. It is so when one realizes a limb of bodhi; then one who is first bringing forth bodhi should learn just so, and from this too it may be known. Cause and effect, earlier and later, are one suchness. Hence it is said that the “citing the fruit to clarify the cause” here contains a twofold meaning.
(Chou) Second, answering and explaining.
[“No, World-Honored One. As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said, when the Buddha was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, there was no dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”]

“No” is a live phrase. It means neither no dharma nor a dharma.
