At that time he had just received the prediction that in the future he would become a Buddha. “Becoming a Buddha” is the name for being granted future realization of the fruit-dharma; hence it is not “no dharma.” Yet at that time it was precisely by realizing the patient acceptance of the non-arising, with not one dharma arising, that he received the prediction; hence it is not “a dharma” either. “Understanding the meaning of what has been said” refers precisely to the meaning stated above, that no dharma brings forth bodhi. It means: by grasping the meaning that no dharma brings forth bodhi, one knows that only with no dharma does one attain bodhi. Why? Because cause and effect are one suchness. The Elder had not yet become a Buddha, nor was he an eighth-ground bodhisattva; how could he know that state? He grasped it only from the meaning the Buddha had spoken. This precisely indicates the importance of the wisdom of understanding. That it says “Buddha” and not “Tathāgata” has a profound meaning. For the “understanding the meaning” above was the grasping, by the meaning of the time of first bringing forth the mind and cultivating the cause, of the mind of one who had realized the eighth-ground fruit. Now, citing “Buddha,” it is by the fruit of having today become a Buddha that he proves the cause of formerly being due to become a Buddha. Why? Because “Buddha” is the title of one who has realized the fruit-dharma and accomplished ultimate enlightenment. In citing the single word “Buddha,” it shows that this is spoken with respect to realized fruition, and that it is not ultimately “no dharma.” Yet by the meaning he had grasped — that only with no dharma does one attain — one may infer: comparing today’s fruit with former causes, it may be known that when he was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha he must not have had the least mental thought of a dharma by which he attained anuttara-bodhi. Pause briefly after “no.” “There is a dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi” was originally the wording of the question. Now adding the word “no” shows that this is spoken with respect to cultivating the cause, and that it is not ultimately “a dharma.” In sum, it reveals that only when the mind has no dharma to seek with can it then be attained. If one dwells in a dharma and seeks to attain, one cannot attain. Hence one should not dwell in dharmas when bringing forth the mind — the meaning is plain.
(Chou) Third, confirming. Two parts: (Yin) First, the Tathāgata’s confirmation and approval; second, explanation by reverse and direct statements.
(Yin) First, the Tathāgata’s confirmation and approval.
[The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is. Subhūti, there is in truth no dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”]

In saying “so it is” twice, he approves his statement that it is neither no dharma nor a dharma as not mistaken. Pause briefly after “in truth no.” “A dharma by which he attained anuttara-bodhi” is to be read continuously. “There is a dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi” was originally the wording of the question. Now the two words “the Tathāgata” are added within it, because Tathāgata is a title of the virtue of the nature. When the enlightened nature is perfect and bright, it is called attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. If there were a dust of dharma, it would not be perfect and bright — how could it be called attaining unsurpassed bodhi? Hence “the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi” is like saying “he attained becoming the Tathāgata.” “There is a dharma by which the Tathāgata attained” and so on is like saying “there is a dharma by which he attained becoming the Tathāgata.” “In truth no” means that at that time, when with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, there was in truth not the least thought of a dharma by which he attained becoming the Tathāgata. That the sutra text does not say “attained becoming the Tathāgata” but must say “the Tathāgata attained anuttara-bodhi” is because it is precisely in the midst of breaking the clinging to dharmas, and so it brings in the unsurpassed bodhi-dharma in speaking. It shows that only because in the causal mind there was in truth no such fruit-dharma did he then attain becoming the Tathāgata. This precisely confirms that the Elder’s understanding is not mistaken. The Elder cited the fruit to clarify the cause, and so spoke of “Buddha.” The World-Honored One, on the other hand, speaks with respect to the virtue of the nature, showing that the enlightened nature is perfect and bright — how could it admit a dharma? Hence he speaks of “the Tathāgata.” His intent is to make one know that only one who attains yet in truth attains nothing is a Tathāgata in whom the virtue of the nature is perfectly manifest. This serves as the premise for what follows — that “Tathāgata” means the suchness of all dharmas.
(Yin) Second, explanation by reverse and direct statements. Two parts: (Mao) First, the reverse explanation; second, the direct explanation.
(Mao) First, the reverse explanation.

[“Subhūti, if there were a dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have given me the prediction: ‘In a future life you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.’”]

These two sections, on explanation by reverse and direct statements, are precisely where the eye was fixed when the question was raised. All that has gone before was based on the fruit-position of the Buddha-ground today to clarify the causal mind of the eighth ground in the past. Here, however, it is based on the fruition-practice of receiving the prediction in the past to clarify the causal mind of one first bringing forth the beginner’s enlightenment today. Hence all that was said above serves as the groundwork for this place. For becoming a Buddha, becoming the Tathāgata, came about through the prediction in the past; and that prediction in the past came about through realizing the non-arising of dharmas. If all bodhisattvas who bring forth the beginner’s enlightenment know that if there is a dharma, no prediction is given, and only with no dharma is the prediction given, then when they receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, they must follow the teaching and, with respect to all dharmas, dwell in non-dwelling. Only thus is their faith not contrary and do they bear the Tathāgata’s burden; only thus can they generate merit, extinguish offenses, and shall attain bodhi. Is not the meaning as plain as if held up to view?

After “saṃbodhi,” the ancient text has no word “one who.” From the statement that no prediction was given, it can be known that this “if there were a dharma by which the Tathāgata attained” and so on refers to the time before the prediction had yet been given. It means: before he received the prediction at that time, had his mind dwelt in the dharma of unsurpassed bodhi, hoping to become the Tathāgata and attain unsurpassed bodhi, then he could not have realized the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, and would not even have obtained the prediction — how much less could he have become the Tathāgata! The three sentences “In a future life ...” are Dīpaṃkara Buddha’s words of prediction. Lest one not understand what a prediction is, they are cited here to explain it. That it does not use the phrase “made this statement” shows that it is not Dīpaṃkara Buddha who is reported as saying this.
(Mao) Second, the direct explanation.

[“Because there is in truth no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, therefore Dīpaṃkara Buddha gave me the prediction, saying, ‘In a future life you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.’”]

Pause after “in truth no.” It means: because in truth there was no mind dwelling in and clinging to the bodhi-dharma in order to seek and attain it. “Therefore” shows that it was precisely because his causal mind had no dharma that he realized the non-arising; for this reason he received the prediction. The phrase “saying” shows that the three sentences “In a future life ...” here were personally uttered by Dīpaṃkara Buddha’s golden mouth, unlike the preceding section, where they were cited to explain the meaning of a prediction.

Some take the meaning of Śākyamuni — Śākya being the surname and Muni the name — to be “able-in-benevolence and still-silence.” Hence they say: being able in benevolence, he does not dwell in nirvāṇa; being still and silent, he does not dwell in birth and death. Because he does not dwell in dharmas, he was given this name in his prediction. This explanation is not unacceptable, but one need not insist on it. For the prediction lays stress on approving his future becoming a Buddha, and has nothing to do with the name. Moreover, every Buddha does not dwell in dharmas, every one receives a prediction from a previous Buddha, and every one has a name, yet their names are not necessarily all taken from the meaning of non-dwelling — how could one rigidly explain it by the name?

What follows is the gist of the section clarifying that every dharma is suchness. The preceding section on attaining without attainment cites the matter of realizing the fruit, in order to clarify that one should not dwell in bodhi; this section on every dharma being suchness states the principle of the realization of the fruit, in order to clarify that there is no bodhi to dwell in. It is precisely the explanation of the reason why one should not dwell. It is the utmost of freedom from marks, and also the original suchness of the nature of dharmas. For in the realization of the fruit, marks and no-marks are alike extinguished. This makes one know that in the practice of the cause, both marks and no-marks should be relinquished together.

The meaning of “every dharma is suchness” is subtle and refined. Let me now first trace its gist to its source and follow it to its end, explaining it in order; then the purport made clear in the sub-sections will have some thread to follow and will be easier to understand. One should know that the World-Honored One spoke this meaning of “every dharma is suchness” in order to enable hearers of the Dharma to understand thoroughly the ultimate, complete teaching. For only when understanding is deep is faith deep, and only when understanding is complete is practice complete; then realization and entry are not difficult. Why? Because as understanding gradually opens, clinging feelings and the view of self gradually dissolve. This is why the study of Buddhism lays stress on the wisdom of understanding. The wisdom of understanding is what is called the wisdom of contemplation. This is why hearing, thinking, and cultivating do not depart from the one wisdom. How then could the gist of “every dharma is suchness” fail to be clearly discerned?

What is called unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is nothing else than the true-suchness nature, also named the intrinsically pure mind. Because it is the source of all dharmas, it is called unsurpassed; because it is commonly possessed by all beings, it is called perfect. It is only that beings are obstructed by false thoughts of discrimination and clinging, and do not themselves know that their nature is unsurpassed and perfect. If they know it and can dispel false thoughts and remove obstructions, then it is called right enlightenment. When one first can be enlightened, it is called bringing forth the beginner’s enlightenment-mind. When enlightenment reaches the ultimate, so that the virtue of the unsurpassed, perfect nature is wholly manifest, there is no way to name it, and it is named the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. In truth the nature is inherently possessed — how could there be any such thing as attainment! This is why, though one attains, it must come down to nothing attained. And one who attains unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, because beings are of one substance with him and because of his original vow of compassion, takes the principle-essence he has personally realized and, with all kinds of words and phrases and all kinds of skillful means, with apt similes and indirect figures, causes all beings universally to be able to awaken to this, understand this, cultivate this, and realize this. There is no way to name it, and it is named the dharma of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. In truth it is the nature inherently possessed by beings — how could there be any such thing as a dharma! Once this principle is understood, one knows that one should not retain the notion of a dharma or the notion of attainment.

Since the intrinsic nature is called pure, it may be known that it is originally unstained by the finest dust. It is like the bright sun in a clear sky: a single fleck of cloud obscures it and it has no light. Hence if one wishes the light of the nature to shine everywhere, one must make it pure without a speck of dust. All beings originally do not know that their intrinsic nature is thus pure. The Buddha, having personally realized it, teaches that one should reflect thus and awaken thus of oneself. If one does not practice in accord with the teaching point by point, how can it be called bringing forth enlightenment? Why? Because if a single dharma remains, if a single attainment remains, it is still the old habit of discrimination and clinging, and one’s original nature remains obstructed. Hence not only should all dharmas not be dwelt in; even the bodhi-dharma should not be dwelt in — for this reason.

Why do beings have the ailment of discrimination and clinging? For no other reason than that they do not penetrate the one true dharma-realm, and only cognize the marks of all dharmas. Since they are marks, mark differs from mark. Because they are deluded about marks, they unknowingly and unwittingly discriminate and cling accordingly. They do not realize that whatever is called a mark is changing at every moment. Hence it is said: “Whatever has marks is illusory and false.” “Illusory and false” means that it is unreal, not true — not that it absolutely does not exist. But beings do not know it is unreal. Thought after thought they discriminate and cling upon illusory marks; hence it is called a false thought, meaning that they pursue illusory marks and give rise to thoughts. Or, though they know it is unreal, still thought after thought does not stop, so that illusory marks churn and disturb the mind; hence it is called a false thought, meaning that illusory marks arise following the thoughts. Thus the single term “false thought” contains these two meanings. The skillful means for counteracting it are likewise two.

(1) Freedom from marks, as stated in the first half of this sutra. One must thoroughly awaken to the fact that all the objective marks of the sense faculties, the body, and the material world are flowers in the sky and moons in the water. To be deluded, cling, and calculate only adds affliction. And one must keep the precepts and cultivate merit, cutting off defiling conditions and removing greed and anger. When contemplation and practice go on thus for a long time, emotional clinging gradually thins, and false thoughts likewise gradually diminish. Why? Because what are called false thoughts are nothing but the work of emotional clinging. Hence freedom from marks is the skillful means for freedom from thoughts — this is one method.

(2) Freedom from thoughts, as stated in the second half of this sutra. For because the habitual tendencies since beginningless time are deep, though one knows that marks are all illusory, one’s climbing and grasping does not cease. One must apply effort at the place where thoughts move, and turn the gaze back upon the source of the mind. All the keeping of precepts, cultivation of merit, the six pāramitās, and the ten thousand practices should be pursued with yet greater vigor, tempering the mind through encountering affairs. If one can strike the thought-process dead, then all discrimination and clinging are of themselves absent, and whether marks exist or not no longer matters. Why? Because if one can refrain from giving rise to thoughts, all marks depart of themselves without departing. Hence freedom from thoughts is the ultimate of freedom from marks — this is another method.
